summary: Describes a way to carry IKE and IPsec packets over a TCP connection so they can traverse middleboxes that block IKE negotiation over UDP. Both the IKE messages and ESP packets are sent inside the TCP connection. It obsoletes RFC 8229. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Some networks block the usual path for secure tunnels. This hides them inside an ordinary TCP connection that the network lets through.

subtitle: How to carry IKE and ESP packets inside one TCP connection when a network blocks UDP.

tldr.problem: Many middleboxes on public hotspots block all UDP traffic, including IKE and IPsec, but let TCP connections through. Devices behind them cannot set up IPsec Security Associations.
tldr.mechanism: Both IKE messages and ESP packets are framed with a 16-bit Length field and sent over a single TCP connection, which starts with the 6-byte stream prefix IKETCP. Support is preconfigured, not negotiated.
tldr.outcome: It is meant as a fallback only: implementations MUST favor direct ESP or UDP encapsulation because TCP adds overhead and performance problems. This document obsoletes RFC 8229.

today: RFC 9329 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2022. It obsoletes RFC 8229, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Put IPsec Inside TCP
sections.content:
IKEv2 sets up IPsec Security Associations (SAs) using IKE messages over UDP, and then protects data with Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) messages. Many middleboxes on public hotspots block all UDP traffic, including IKE and IPsec, but allow TCP connections because they look like web traffic. Devices on those networks then cannot establish IPsec SAs.

RFC 9329 defines a way to encapsulate IKE control messages and ESP data messages within a TCP connection. It lists this as a third option next to direct use (IKE on UDP port 500) and UDP encapsulation (UDP port 4500, described in RFC 3948). Authentication Header (AH) is not supported.

The document obsoletes RFC 8229. It clarifies the Length field, NAT detection, retransmission, cookies and puzzles, error handling and the interaction with MOBIKE, and adds TLS 1.3 to the TLS recommendations and examples.
sections.eli5: If the front door is locked, you use the side door that is still open. This document describes how to use the side door for secure tunnels.

sections.title: Framing IKE and ESP Messages
sections.content:
TCP is a byte stream, so each message needs a boundary. TCP encapsulation puts a 16-bit Length field in network byte order before every message. Its value is the length of the original message plus the length of the field itself, in octets. Like UDP encapsulation, the first 4 bytes of the message tell IKE from ESP: if the first 32 bits are zeros (a non-ESP marker), the content is an IKE message, otherwise it is an ESP message.

Because the Length field is 16 bits and counts itself, messages larger than 65533 octets cannot be encapsulated. A Length of 0 or 1 is a fatal error and the receiver MUST close the TCP connection. Empty messages, where Length equals 2, MUST be silently ignored. In an ESP packet the SPI MUST NOT be zero.

Every stream also begins with a fixed 6-byte magic value, the characters IKETCP in ASCII. It is sent once, only by the TCP Originator, at the start of the stream. It identifies the connection as TCP encapsulation as defined here and avoids conflicts with earlier non-standard protocols that used TCP port 4500.
sections.eli5: Because a TCP connection is just one long line of bytes, each message gets a label saying how long it is. The very first thing sent is a secret handshake word, IKETCP, so both sides know what game is being played.

sections.title: Configuration and Falling Back from UDP
sections.content:
Support for TCP encapsulation is not negotiated in IKE. It must be preconfigured on both the TCP Originator (the peer that opens the TCP connection) and the TCP Responder. Compliant implementations MUST support TCP port 4500. Optional settings include alternate listening ports on the Responder and an extra framing protocol such as TLS on top of TCP.

UDP stays the preferred transport. An Initiator with no prior knowledge of the network SHOULD try IKE over UDP first, retransmitting the initial message at least once, and can move to TCP after hitting the maximum retransmissions, or slightly before. When switching, a new IKE_SA_INIT exchange MUST be started with a new SPI and recalculated NAT_DETECTION_*_IP notifications.

Once TCP encapsulation is used for an IKE SA, all IKE messages and the ESP packets of its Child SAs MUST travel over the TCP connection until the SA is deleted or MOBIKE changes the endpoints or the encapsulation.
sections.eli5: You always knock on the normal door first. Only after nobody answers do you try the side door, and both sides must already have agreed that the side door exists.

sections.title: Connections and Teardown
sections.content:
The Originator opens a TCP connection to the Responder's preconfigured port and sends the stream prefix first. The Responder MUST wait for the entire prefix before parsing any IKE or ESP message. IKE SAs should be closed with DELETE payloads, after which the Originator SHOULD close the TCP connection if it will not reuse it.

An unexpected FIN or TCP Reset may mean lost connectivity or an attack, so both sides SHOULD keep SA state for the normal lifetime or timeout. The Originator re-establishes a broken connection, sends the stream prefix again, and the Responder MUST accept packets for existing SAs from new source addresses and ports. Multiple IKE SAs MUST NOT share a TCP connection, except temporarily when one is a rekey of the other.

If a connection is corrupted, for example by many messages that cannot be parsed or by failed authentication checks, either side SHOULD close it. A syntax error inside an IKE message is handled with an INVALID_SYNTAX notification, not by dropping the TCP connection.
sections.eli5: One tunnel uses one line. If the line drops, the side that started it picks the phone up again and says the secret word first.

sections.title: Retransmissions, Cookies and NAT Handling
sections.content:
TCP is already reliable, so the usual IKE retransmission rules change. The exchange Initiator SHOULD NOT retransmit requests, and if no response arrives in a reasonable time the IKE SA is deleted. If a new TCP connection is set up while it waits, it MUST retransmit its request over the new connection.

IKEv2 cookies protect a Responder from holding state for spoofed addresses, but over TCP the address is already verified by the handshake, and the TCP stack keeps state after a SYN anyway. So a Responder SHOULD NOT send a Cookie request without an accompanying Puzzle, and it MUST NOT include the Initiator's TCP port in the cookie calculation. The RFC believes that 5-10 seconds is a good compromise for how long to keep the connection open after a cookie reply.

IKE_SA_INIT packets over TCP SHOULD still include the NAT detection payloads, using the TCP ports. A detected NAT changes nothing about encapsulation, since TCP traverses NATs inherently. IPsec NAT-keepalive packets SHOULD NOT be sent, but they MUST be silently dropped if received; liveness is checked with IKE informational messages, not TCP or TLS keepalives.
sections.eli5: Since TCP already promises delivery, you do not need to keep shouting the same message. And you check your friend is still there by asking in the tunnel, not by listening for the phone line hum.

sections.title: Interaction with IKEv2 Extensions
sections.content:
With MOBIKE, a client that moves networks may switch between TCP encapsulation, UDP encapsulation and none. Implementations that support both MUST be able to enable and disable TCP encapsulation dynamically. The UPDATE_SA_ADDRESSES exchange SHOULD be tried over UDP first, then repeated over TCP if there is no answer, without starting a new INFORMATIONAL exchange. The NO_NATS_ALLOWED notification SHOULD be ignored over TCP, and the Return Routability Check SHOULD NOT be performed, since a TCP handshake already proves the address.

After an IKE redirect or session resumption, the client chooses its transport afresh, trying UDP first and then TCP. IKE fragmentation is not needed over TCP; an implementation SHOULD NOT send fragments over TCP but MUST be able to receive them.

For high availability clusters, state is harder to share over TCP. A client that is a TCP Originator SHOULD periodically send IKEv2 messages, such as a liveness check, whenever there is no IKEv2 or ESP traffic, so a failover is detected and the connection restored.
sections.eli5: When your phone moves from one Wi-Fi to another, it tries the fast route first and only falls back to the slower hidden route if the fast one is blocked again.

sections.title: Performance Costs
sections.content:
Implementations MUST favor direct ESP or UDP encapsulation over TCP whenever possible. The main problem is TCP-in-TCP: if the tunnel is a TCP connection and the traffic inside is also TCP, loss on the outer connection is hidden and shows up only as delay. That can cause spurious retransmissions in the inner connection and lower its sending rate. The RFC also describes TCP meltdown, where the two layers' retransmissions make each other worse, and says the higher layer should have a much longer timeout than the lower one.

ESP is normally unreliable, so retransmission by TCP can hurt applications such as Voice over IP that prefer loss to delay. Individual packets SHOULD NOT carry different QoS markings from the rest of the connection, and the connection SHOULD negotiate its MSS to avoid fragmentation. For ECN, implementations SHOULD follow the compatibility mode of RFC 6040, in which the outer TCP connection is marked not ECN-capable.
sections.eli5: It is like putting a delivery truck inside another delivery truck. Each truck tries to fix delays on its own, and together they can get in each other's way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A Responder that supports TCP encapsulation becomes exposed to TCP-specific denial-of-service attacks such as SYN flooding, and to RST and other spoofing attacks. Injection of data into the TCP stream cannot change application data because IPsec provides integrity, but altering a Length field makes the receiver lose track of message boundaries and drop following packets. Recovery can take several minutes and may delete and re-create the IKE SA.

To speed recovery, implementations are advised to close the TCP connection when packets carry SPIs that match no known SA, or MAY try to resync by searching the stream for a known SPI and valid sequence number and checking the ICV. An attacker who can block UDP can force peers onto TCP encapsulation, with its performance and DoS exposure. Responders must validate new connections with decryption, authentication and replay checks before moving traffic to them.

Appendix A adds that when TLS is used only for encapsulation, the security of the IKE session still comes entirely from IKE, so both sides SHOULD allow the NULL cipher for performance, and it is RECOMMENDED to follow RFC 9325 when choosing TLS parameters.
sections.eli5: An attacker cannot read or change what is inside the tunnel, but could mess with the labels on the outside and make the receiver confused for a while.
